# nacatamalon

> A 2D and 3D game engine for the web, in TypeScript, on WebGPU with a WebGL2 fallback, aimed at
> the look of the consoles from the SNES to the GameCube. A scene is a function; it asks for what it
> needs with hooks, and what it creates is plain data you change.

This is the short guide. `llms-full.txt`, next to this file, is the full reference: every export
with its signature and documentation, each under a `### name` heading. Search it for any name below.

Worked examples, one per feature with all their code: https://nacatamalon.com/llms/examples.md lists
them by topic, each with an id, and `https://nacatamalon.com/llms/examples/<id>.md` is one of them.

## The mental model

- A **scene** is a function that runs **once**, when the scene starts. It creates things and
  registers what happens later, then returns `createScene()`.
- **Hooks** (`use*`) work only while a scene, or something spawned with `useSpawn`, is being built.
  Call them at the top of the function and keep what they return.
- **`create*` returns plain data.** Change its fields and the next frame shows it:
  `sprite.transform.x += 1`, `sprite.tint = getColor('red')`, `text.text = 'SCORE 10'`.
- **`useUpdate((delta, time) => { ... })`** runs every frame. `delta` is seconds since the last frame,
  capped at 0.25; `time` is seconds since the scene started. With `createGame({ step: 60 })` (`50`
  for PAL) a frame is a fixed step instead: `delta` is always `1/60`, whatever the screen's rate, so a
  jump is the same height everywhere and `x += 2` is two pixels a frame. Use it for anything tuned
  frame by frame (platformers, shooters); without it, frames follow the screen.
- What acts on a thing is a function that takes it first: `destroy(sprite)`. What a hook returns is a
  handle with methods: `keys.isDown('ArrowLeft')`, `useScene().change('Level')`.
- Files load in the background. `useLoadTexture` and the other loaders return at once, and what uses
  the file appears when it arrives. `useLoader()` reports progress.
- **A game with music or several scenes starts with a loading scene**: a `Preload` scene asks for
  what the game uses (`useLoader([useLoadTexture(...), useLoadSong(...)])`), shows its bar, and
  changes to the first real scene when `loader.done`. What is loaded is the game's, not the scene's:
  a later scene asks for the same file by the same name and has it at once, so no scene after it
  waits.
- **It looks like React and is not.** Nothing is rendered again: a scene, or a piece made with
  `useSpawn`, runs its body once, and changing its state or its props does not run it again. What
  changes over time is done by hand, in `useUpdate`, or in `useWatch(fn, [data])` when a value
  changes. `useData` is not `useState`: its setter tells the watchers, and the body stays as it was.
  Keep the objects `create*` gives back and change their fields; never make them again to update
  them.

## A whole game

```ts
import { createGame, createScene, createSprite, createText, getColor, useKeyboard, useUpdate } from 'nacatamalon';

const Game = () => {
    const keys = useKeyboard();
    const paddle = createSprite({ width: 64, height: 10, tint: getColor('#ff6b1a'), transform: { x: 240, y: 300 } });
    const score = createText({ text: 'SCORE 0', transform: { x: 8, y: 8 } });
    let points = 0;

    useUpdate((delta) => {
        if (keys.isDown('ArrowLeft')) {
            paddle.transform.x -= 340 * delta;
        }
        if (keys.isDown('ArrowRight')) {
            paddle.transform.x += 340 * delta;
        }
        // The anchor is the middle, so the paddle's edges are half its width away.
        const half = paddle.width / 2;
        paddle.transform.x = Math.min(Math.max(paddle.transform.x, half), 480 - half);
        if (keys.justPressed('Space')) {
            points += 10;
            score.text = 'SCORE ' + points;
        }
    });

    return createScene();
};

// The page needs <div id="app"></div>. The first scene in the object starts.
createGame('#app', { width: 480, height: 320, background: getColor('#12102b') })({ Game });
```

## Conventions

- **2D is pixels**, origin at the top-left of the game, y grows down. With no `useCamera2d`, `x`
  and `y` are positions on the screen. **3D is y-up**; give every 3D scene a `useCamera3d`.
- **3D next to 2D**: `useCamera3d()` is orthographic by default and measures in the same pixels as
  the 2D, but its origin is the **bottom-left** corner and y grows **up**. A model placed where a
  sprite is takes `x` as it is and `y = HEIGHT - y2d` (`HEIGHT` the game's height). It sees `far`
  (default 1000) in front of and behind the camera, so a model around `z = 0` is drawn; `zIndex`
  orders models and sprites together. A perspective camera (`projection: 'perspective'`) needs a
  `z` to stand back from what it looks at.
- **Canvas size**: `createGame` `width` and `height` are the game's size, and by default (`scaling:
  'none'`) the canvas is shown at exactly that size; it does not fit the page. Pass `scaling:
  'integer'` (whole multiples, crisp pixel art) or `'contain'` (as large as fits).
- **Splash**: off unless asked for. `createGame` `splash: true` opens the published game with
  "Made with NacatamalOn" for under two seconds while the first scene loads behind it; it is
  skipped on `localhost` and in automated browsers, so development and tests never see it.
  `splash: 'always'` shows it there too.
- **Sprite anchor** defaults to the middle, `{ x: 0.5, y: 0.5 }`: `transform` places the centre.
  `{ x: 0, y: 0 }` places the top-left corner, `{ x: 0.5, y: 1 }` the feet.
- **Text anchor** defaults to the top-left corner, `{ x: 0, y: 0 }`. `{ x: 0.5, y: 0 }` centres it on
  `x`; `{ x: 1, y: 0 }` puts its right edge on `x` (a score at the right of the screen);
  `{ x: 0.5, y: 0.5 }` centres it both ways on the point. The two differ on purpose: a thing of the
  world sits by its middle, the point it turns and grows on; a text by its corner, so it grows without
  moving (a score going from 9 to 10 does not shift). A panel (`createNineSlice`) sits by its middle,
  like a sprite. A label centred on a panel gives both the same anchor.
- **How big, and where**: `sizeOf(thing)` is a sprite's, a text's or a panel's width and height with
  its own scale (a sprite's picture when it was given no size, a text's letters, measured the moment
  it is made); `boundsOf(thing)` the rectangle it covers, `{ x, y, width, height }` from its top-left
  corner, anchor and pivot taken into account, in the place its `transform` is written: a box behind a
  label, `coin.transform.x = boundsOf(score).x + boundsOf(score).width + 4`.
- **Pivot**: a sprite, a text or a panel turns and grows about its anchor, unless `pivot` (0-1, like
  `anchor`) names another point. The anchor says where it sits, the pivot what it spins on: a bike
  anchored under its back wheel (`anchor: { x: 5 / 24, y: 1 }`) wheelies about it, and set
  `bike.pivot = { x: 0.5, y: 0.5 }` while it crashes to spin about its middle without moving off;
  `bike.pivot = undefined` turns it about the wheel again. Unturned and ungrown it sits as its anchor
  says. It turns about it when its own transform turns or its box's (a behaviour turning `self`);
  boxes further up carry it as one. No sine, cosine or offset by hand, and no extra box.
- **Sprite size**: a sprite created with both `width` and `height` has them as numbers. A sprite
  sized by its picture (a `texture`, no `width`/`height`) has them `undefined`, and they stay so: it
  is drawn at the size of what it shows, which is `texture.width * (uvScale?.x ?? 1)` (and the same
  for the height) once the picture has loaded, one frame of a sheet and not the whole sheet.
- **Keys** are `KeyboardEvent.key` names: letters lowercase (`'a'`), named keys as they are
  (`'ArrowLeft'`, `'Enter'`, `'Escape'`). The space bar is `'Space'`; `' '` also works.
- **Text** needs no font: `createText({ text })` uses the built-in 8 px font, which has lowercase,
  accents, ñ, ¿ and ¡, and for prompts `← → ↑ ↓ ▲ ▼ ◀ ▶ Ⓐ Ⓑ Ⓧ Ⓨ ★ ♥ ● ■` (`'PRESS ▶'`); two more
  built in, with the same characters, are named by key, nothing loaded: `font: 'nacatamalon:square'`,
  `font: 'nacatamalon:thin'` (also in `drawText`). `style.fontSize` is the line height in pixels; multiples of 8 stay crisp. A
  font of your own, passed as `font`: `useLoadFont({ src: '/fonts/x.ttf' })` for a `.ttf`/`.woff`
  (sharp at any size; `fontSize` is the em size as in CSS; no `.otf` with cubic outlines or `.woff2`),
  or `useLoadBitmapFont({ json, atlas })` for a bitmap font (an image plus a JSON of glyph positions).
  A font loaded with a `key` in an earlier scene is named by it, `createText({ text, font: 'title' })`,
  with no loader in that scene.
- **Mouse look** (first person): `usePointer().lock()` captures the mouse, but only when called from
  a click or key press (`pointer.onDown(() => { void pointer.lock(); })`); then turn the camera with
  `movementX`/`movementY` from `onMove`, which keep changing while `screenX`/`screenY` do not.
  `isLocked()` turns `false` when the player presses Esc.
- **Touch** (phones): an on-screen button is an ordinary component that says which action it presses,
  `useTouchAction('jump')` in its body: the action is held while a finger is on it, so the game still
  reads `actions.isDown('jump')`, and one `Button` component made twice with two props is two buttons
  (`useSpawn(Button)({ x: 400, action: 'jump' })`). A project's map binds a button of a scene by its
  name instead, `{ type: 'touch', box: 'Jump' }`. Draw it with the
  engine, never as HTML over the canvas (the native runtime has no page). `usePointer()` also answers
  `isDown()`, `justPressed()` and `justReleased()` (one frame, like the keyboard; `justPressed('right')` for
  one button, the names in `INPUT.POINTER_BUTTONS`; a right click opens no browser menu over the game unless
  `contextMenu: true`, or `useGame().setContextMenu(true)` while it runs), `position()`, `touches()` (each finger, by `pointerId`) and `isPressing(sprite)`. How long
  an action has been held, for a charged shot: `actions.heldFor('fire')`, still set on its
  `justReleased` frame.
- **When a press happened**, to the moment of the hand and not of the frame (up to a frame earlier),
  in seconds on the page's clock: `keys.pressedAt('Space')`, `pointer.pressedAt()`, `pad.pressedAt('a')`,
  `actions.pressedAt('hit')` (each `null` unless `justPressed`), and `time` in every pointer event. A rhythm game judges it against
  the song: `song.positionAt(keys.pressedAt('Space'))` (after checking it is not `null`) is the moment of
  the song being heard then. No listeners on `window` of its own: the native runtime has none.
- **Where something is goes in `transform`**, for everything placed in the world, lights and cameras
  too: `useCamera3d({ transform: { z: 5 }, fov: 60 })`, `useSpotLight({ transform: { y: 4, rotationX:
  -1.2 }, range: 8 })`, read back as `camera.transform.z`. A light with none is where its object is.
- **An asset's `key`** (every `useLoad…`) is the name the game finds it by, here or in a later scene;
  without one, its `src`. `createSprite({ texture: 'hero' })` and `createText({ font: 'title' })` name
  it. One key names one file: asking for another file under a key already taken says so and hands back
  the first.
- **Time is in seconds**, everywhere: `delta`, timers (`timer.after(0.5)`), tweens, animations,
  transitions (`fade(0.3)`, not `fade(300)`), a pad's `rumble({ duration: 0.2 })`, a store's `throttle`.
- **Angles are in radians** (`Math.PI / 2` is a quarter turn; `degToRad(90)` if you think in degrees):
  every `rotation`, a spot light's `angle`, particles' `spread` and `spin`. Three are in degrees, as
  everyone says them: a 3D camera's `fov` (`60`), a `hue` (0 to 360 in `fromHsl`, -180 to 180 in
  `colorAdjust`), and a sound's `cone`.
- **A screen effect's call takes what a person writes**: points `{ x, y }` (`distort({ center: { x:
  0.5, y: 0.5 } })`), modes by name (`halftone({ mode: 'lines' })`, `wave({ axis: 'columns' })`), yes or no
  as booleans (`grain({ animated: false })`). Its `effect.uniforms` are what the shader reads: numbers
  and `[x, y]`, which is what a project file keeps and a motion moves.
- **Colours** are `{ r, g, b, a }`, each 0 to 1. `getColor` takes `'#ff6b1a'`, `0xff6b1a`, a CSS
  name (`'red'`) or any CSS colour (`'rgba(255, 0, 0, 0.5)'`, `'hsl(30 100% 50%)'`). Every option that
  takes a colour takes the same (`createSprite({ tint: '#ff6b1a' })`, `usePointLight({ color: 'orange'
  })`, `fade(0.3, 'white')`, `setBackground('#000')`); what is read back (`sprite.tint`) is always `{ r,
  g, b, a }`, so assigning one is `sprite.tint = getColor('red')`.
  To blend two colours (a sky between dusk and night), `lerpColor(a, b, t)`.
- **Glows, flashes, beams of light**: `createSprite({ ..., blend: 'additive' })` (a text or a panel too) adds its colour to
  what is behind instead of covering it, the same as additive particles.
- **A placed model is used like any drawing**: what `createModel(...)` returns has `visible`, `tint`,
  `alpha`, `zIndex` and `castShadow` for every piece at once, set any time, even before the file
  arrives (its pieces arrive so); `destroy(model)` takes it all. `parts` is for one piece alone (the
  glass of a car).
- **Particle effects that depend on the game** (dust the colour of the ground, a tint per level):
  write the effect in code, `createParticles({ effect: { kind: 'particles-2d', emission: { rate: 30 },
  colorOverLife: [{ t: 0, color: lerpColor(a, b, t) }], texture: createPixelTexture(puff) } })`, with
  the fields of a `.particles` file; it is ready at once. Pass the same object to share one effect.
- **Angles** are radians.
- **Types** come from the same imports as the functions, all starting with `T`:
  `import type { TSprite, TText } from 'nacatamalon';`.
- **Scenes** are registered by name: `createGame(...)({ Title, Level })`, an object, not an array.
  `useScene().change('Level')` starts `Level` and stops the current scene: its objects are removed
  and its `useUpdate` stops. Changing back runs that scene's function again from the start, so
  anything kept in its local variables or `useData` starts over.
- **A scene takes props**, how it is opened: `const Level = ({ level = 1 }: { level?: number }) =>
  ...`, then `useScene().change(Level, { props: { level: 3 } })` (or `launch(Hud, { props })`). By the
  function TypeScript checks them; by name it does not. Every prop needs a default: the first scene,
  a restart and the editor's Play start it with none. What stays true across scenes (lives, coins)
  is a store, not a prop.
- **`change()` acts at once, but the frame it is called in finishes**: the code after it and the old
  scene's other `useUpdate` callbacks still run that one frame, then never again. `return` right
  after `change()` if the rest should not run. The new scene's first update is the next frame, so the
  key that caused the change is not a fresh `justPressed` there.
- **Pictures generated in code, instead of a `<canvas>`**: drawn art (characters, tiles, backgrounds)
  is made in a pixel-art editor and loaded with `useLoadTexture`. When a picture has to be *generated*
  instead (procedural variations, a placeholder, noise or a mask for a shader, a picture that changes
  while the game runs, or art made by an agent with no image editor), use `createPixels` and paint it
  with `fillRect`, `drawLine`, `fillCircle`, `fillEllipse`, `fillPolygon`, `fillGradient`, `fillNoise`, `blitPixels`,
  `mapPixels`...; write on it with `drawText(pixels, 'MOTEL', x, y, { color, font?, fontSize?, anchor? })`
  (no font: the built-in one, needing nothing; a loaded font must have arrived, so in the scene that
  loads it draw inside `useWatch(..., [font])` then `updatePixelTexture`), rather than hand-making a
  pixel font. Then `createPixelTexture(pixels)` in the scene body gives a texture for `createSprite({ texture })`
  or `createMaterial({ texture })`. **Do not draw on a `<canvas>`** (`document.createElement('canvas')`,
  `getContext('2d')`, `getImageData`): it only exists in a browser, and the native runtime has no page;
  the pixels functions run everywhere. Paint on the picture again and `updatePixelTexture(texture,
  region)` shows it, at any time. A build script saves one as a file with `encodePng` from
  `nacatamalon/authoring`.
- **Processing a drawn picture in code**: to *show* a PNG, `useLoadTexture`. To *read or change* it
  first (a palette swap, a white hit silhouette, an outline, a collision mask, a level read from an
  image), `useLoadPixels({ src })`, decoded with no canvas; hand it to `createPixelTexture(loaded,
  (p) => swapColors(p, [[from, to]]))`, which returns at once and fills in when the file lands, painting
  on a copy. The loaded `pixels` are shared: read them (`getPixel`), never paint on them directly.
- **Photos taken by the game** (a photography game, an album, a sticker of the boss): `const capture =
  useCapture()` in the body, then at any moment `const photo = await capture({ region, hide, only,
  width, height, effects })`. `region` is a rectangle of the screen in game pixels or a box (by name
  too), the part of the screen it covers even hidden (a viewfinder); `hide` leaves boxes out (the
  HUD); `only` keeps some alone on transparent; `width`/`height` scale by whole pixels; `effects:
  false` is under the screen effects. `photo` is pixels plus `photo.boxes`: each sprite, text or
  panel shown in the frame (its `box`, `picture` and `name`) with `seen` (0 to 1) and where, for
  scoring; a box with hitboxes counts once, by them. To show it, make the print in the body
  (`createPixels`, `createPixelTexture`, a sprite) and later `film.data.set(photo.data);
  updatePixelTexture(print)`. Do not read the canvas yourself.
- **Data that outlives a scene** goes in a store, created once at module level:
  `const session = createGameStore({ key: 'session', state: { score: 0 } });`, then
  `session.set((s) => { s.score += 10; })` in one scene and `session.state.score` in the next.
  `key` is required and must be unique per game: two stores with one key warn, and the later replaces
  the earlier.

## Gotchas

- A hook called inside `useUpdate`, an event handler, a timeout or after `await` throws
  `[NacatamalOn] <hook>: call it inside a scene body...`. Create everything up front and change
  `visible`, or spawn things with `useSpawn`.
- An object is built before the objects inside it: a body (or a script on a scene document's root)
  that looks for a child with `findObject` finds `null`. Look it up inside
  `useReady(() => { ... })`, which runs once everything being built with it exists, before the
  first frame.
- Movement without `* delta` runs faster on screens with a higher refresh rate, unless the game has a
  `step`.
- `useUpdate` runs a scene before the objects inside it, so a camera (or a marker, a shadow) that
  copies another object's position there reads it one frame late and shakes. Follow things in
  `useLateUpdate`, which runs after every `useUpdate`; move them in `useUpdate`.
- `createGame` with no matching element throws: the page needs the element before the script runs.
- Physics is behind its own imports and is switched on once: `installPhysics2d()` from
  `nacatamalon/physics2d`, or `installPhysics3d()` from `nacatamalon/physics3d`. The physics engines
  are included in the package: there is nothing else to install.
- A `'static'` body never moves. Something that moves and pushes others (a platform, a moving peg) is
  `body: 'kinematic'`, moved with `setLinearVelocity` on its handle, which is
  `getPhysicsWorld2d()?.bodyOf(useSelf())` (or `getPhysicsWorld3d`) taken while the object is built.
  The handle's `setLayers(layer, collidesWith)` changes what it collides with, and its `destroy()`
  removes the body and keeps the object. `destroy(object)` removes the object's body too.
- Physics layers have names when the game gives them: `createGame(…, { physicsLayers: ['world',
  'player', 'enemy'] })` (or `physicsLayers` in `project.json`), the first is layer 0; then a body
  says `layer: 'enemy', collidesWith: ['world', 'player']`, and `setLayers('ghost', [])` the same.
  Two bodies meet only if each one's `collidesWith` has the other's layer.

## Talking between pieces

A game is small pieces made with `useSpawn`, and each way they talk has one job:

| To... | Use |
|---|---|
| keep a value of this piece that others watch (lives, a level's points) | `useData`, read with `useWatch` |
| keep a value of the whole game, across scenes or saved (best score, settings) | `createGameStore`; `useStore` to react to one value of it, `useWatch(fn, [store, lives])` to draw from it and more |
| say something happened, for anyone to hear (`gameOver`) | `createGameSignal`, `useSignal` |
| tell whoever placed you (an enemy dead, a button pressed) | a callback in your props: `useSpawn(Enemy)({ onDied })`. From a pack or a behaviour, which take only data: `useReport('pressed')` sends it up, `onReport(copy, 'pressed', h)` or a pack's `on` hears it |
| tell a piece you made what to do (`hurt`, `open`) | the `api` it returns: `useSpawn(Bat)({ x }).api.hurt(1)` |
| let two behaviours on the same box talk | return an api from one, `useScriptApi(name)` in the other; `provide(word, api)` for a word several behaviours answer to |
| find everything of a kind (every coin left) | a tag: `useTag('coin').all()` |
| reach something you did not make (a box of a saved scene) | `findObject(sceneOf(self), 'Score')` |

A signal is imported by both sides and every listener hears every one; a report needs nothing in
common and reaches only the first one above that listens, so three copies of a pack's button are
three things to tell apart. Not a module `let`: it is not reset when the scene starts again.

## React

`nacatamalon/react` puts a game in a React page, with the HUD and menus written as React components
drawn over the canvas. The game itself is still scenes; React never goes inside a scene.

```tsx
import { Game, useGame, useGameStore, useSignal } from 'nacatamalon/react';

const Hud = () => {
    const hunger = useGameStore(petStore, (s) => s.hunger); // a value; the component renders again
    const game = useGame(); // TGameHandle, or null while the renderer starts
    return <button onClick={() => game?.pause('menu')}>{Math.round(hunger)}</button>;
};

const App = () => (
    <Game options={{ width: 320, height: 224 }} scenes={{ Level }}>
        <Hud /> {/* position it with position: absolute */}
    </Game>
);
```

- **Two sides, two rules.** A scene body runs once: in it, `useStore(store, selector, handler)` from
  `nacatamalon` runs a handler. A component renders again: in it, `useGameStore(store, selector)`
  from `nacatamalon/react` returns the value. `useGame` and `useSignal` have the same names on both
  sides; import them from `nacatamalon` in a scene and from `nacatamalon/react` in a component.
- **Select values, not objects**: the state is changed in place, so `(s) => s.items` never looks
  changed. `(s) => s.items.length` does.
- `<Game>` reads `options` and `scenes` once. Give it a new `key` to start a new game.
- **Browser only**: the native (desktop) runtime shows only what the engine draws, so a React HUD is
  not on screen there. A game meant to ship natively builds its HUD with `createText`, sprites and
  `createNineSlice`.

## Where things are (search llms-full.txt for each name)

- **Constants**: on the root, in groups, read only and frozen (writing into one throws): `import { LIMITS, BUILTIN } from 'nacatamalon'`. `RENDER` (`TYPE.WEBGL2`… for `createGame({ renderer })`, `LINE_VERTEX_FLOATS`), `INPUT` (`GAMEPAD_BUTTONS`, `GAMEPAD_AXES` and their `…_LABELS`, `POINTER_BUTTONS`, `DEADZONE`, `ACTION_PRESS`), `LIMITS` (`LIGHTS`, `PHYSICS_LAYERS`, `PALETTE_COLORS`), `PHYSICS` (`ALL_LAYERS`), `POST` (`CRT_PRESETS`, `COLOR_LEVELS`), `BUILTIN` (what the engine carries, by kind: `FONTS`, `MUSIC.SONGS`, `MUSIC.INSTRUMENTS`, `MUSIC.SAMPLES`, `SOUNDS`, `POST`, `LOOKS`). A game carries only the groups it reads.
- **Game and scenes**: `createGame`, `createScene`, `useScene`, `useGame`, `useSpawn` (what the component returns is the object's `api`: `useSpawn(Bat)({ x: 200 }).api.hurt(1)`; a name for what it makes, when something finds it by name, `useSpawn(Bat, 'Bat')`: the function's own is shortened by a published build), `useSelf`, `sceneOf` and `findObject` (the scene something is in, and a box of it by name, destroyed ones left out: `findObject(sceneOf(self), 'Score')`), `destroy`, `useReady`, `useCleanup` (runs when its component is destroyed or its scene stops: for a window listener or an interval; what the engine made needs none).
- **Tags**: what something is, `'enemy'`, `'coin'`, as many as it likes: `useTag('enemy')` gives the tag, to `add(thing)`, `remove`, `has`, `all()` (everything in the scene carrying it) and `clear()`; a piece adds itself with `useTag('enemy').add(useSelf())`, or is made with `useSpawn(Bat, { tags: ['enemy'] })`; a sprite, text or panel can carry tags on its own (`createSprite({ tags: ['wall'] })`). A saved scene's box keeps them (`"tags": [...]`).
- **Touching, with no physics**: `collisionBetween(a, b)`; `useHitbox({ width?, height? })` (the picture's size by default; change `x`, `y`, `width`, `height`, `enabled` any time); collisions are asked by component or by tag: `useCollisionWith(Enemy, (enemy) => enemy.api.hurt(1))` in a piece's own body meets the pieces made from `Enemy`, their `api` typed; `useCollisionWith('damageable', (thing) => ...)` meets everything carrying the tag, pieces and tagged sprites alike (`'api' in thing` tells which). `{ when: 'start' }` once, `'end'` on parting; every frame by default. So a bullet and an enemy written apart need no rule in the scene; `useCollisionBetween(Shot, Enemy, (shot, enemy) => ...)` (components or tags) is a rule of the scene, every frame each pair touches. Both run after the updates and measure a piece by its hitboxes (or what it draws) and a tagged sprite by itself; two pieces with physics bodies (2D or 3D) also meet when the simulation says they touch, so the same line works with or without physics.
- **Points on an object**: `worldToLocal(object, point)` and `localToWorld(object, point)` (a sprite works too), `worldToLocal3d` and `localToWorld3d`; the pointer's `worldX`/`worldY` are the world they mean.
- **Time**: `useUpdate`, `useLateUpdate`, `useTimer`, `useTween`, easings such as `linear` and `easeInOutSine`.
- **Input**: `useKeyboard`, `usePointer`, `useGamepad`, `useActions`, `useAction`, `useTouchAction`.
- **2D**: `createSprite`, `useLoadTexture`, `useLoadAtlas`, `useSpriteAnimation`, `createText`, `useLoadFont`, `useLoadBitmapFont`, `createNineSlice`, `createTilemap`, `tileAt`, `solidAt`, `tileInfoAtPoint`, `createParticles`, `useCamera2d`.
- **Platformer tiles** (fields of a tile in the `.tilemap`, read with `tileInfoAt`/`tileInfoAtPoint`): `oneWay` (a ledge, stood on from above), `ladder`, `slope: [left, right]` (floor heights 0 to 1), `damage` (a value the game interprets; the engine never applies it), `push: { x, y }` (pixels per second), and `props` for anything else (`{ water: true }`). A ledge or slope leaves `solid` off.
- **3D**: `createMesh`, `useCubeGeometry`, `usePlaneGeometry`, `useUvSphereGeometry`, `createMaterial`, `useLoadGltf`, `createModel`, `useSkeletalAnimation` (of the model `createModel` gave back, `useSkeletalAnimation(fox, { play: 'Walk' })`: each placed model has bones of its own), `useCamera3d`, `cameraLookAt`, `useDirectionalLight`, `usePointLight`, `useSpotLight`, `useRectLight` (a panel: `width`, `height`, `range`, facing down unless turned, no shadows), `useBlobShadow`, `createParticles3d`.
- **Material maps** (extra pictures for a model's shader): `createMaterial({ shader: 'mesh3d', texture, maps: { noise, env }, fragment })` carries up to 4 named maps; the shader reads one with `sampleMap_<name>(uv)` (`sampleMap_noise(ctx.uv)`), and `envUv(ctx)` gives the coordinates of a chrome reflection (`sampleMap_env(envUv(ctx))`). A map the material lacks reads white. In the shader composer, `composerMapSample(name, uv)`, `composerEnvUv()` and `composerShine()` (prefer the composer: it writes both shader languages from one graph).
- **Material looks** (a model's look without writing a shader): `createMaterial({ shader: 'mesh3d', tint, lighting: toonLighting({ bands: 2 }), steps: [mangaDots(), rim({ color: '#ffd966' })] })`. `lighting` is one of `toonLighting()` or `unlitLighting()`; `steps` are `mangaDots()` and `rim()`, in order. Also `createModel({ model, lighting, steps })` (every piece, bones included) and `compileShader({ shader: 'mesh3d', lighting, steps })`. Their numbers are knobs: `material.uniforms.toonShadow`, `mangaDotsSize`, `rimColor`. Not with `fragment` or `effect`.
- **What a model's material reads** (`fn effect(surface, ctx: FragContext)`): `uv`, `normal`, `worldPos`, `viewDir`, `light`, `shine`, `emissive`, `color`, `screen` (the pixel's place on the screen in game pixels, top left `(0, 0)`: for dot screens and hatches that stay put), `tangent` and `bitangent` (the way across and down the surface the picture runs, in the world: for relief and ripples) and `uv2` (a second picture coordinate, the file's `TEXCOORD_1` or `uv` again). In the composer: `composerScreenPos()`, `composerUv2()`, `composerWorldTangent()`, `composerWorldBitangent()`, `composerVertexTangent()`, `composerVertexBitangent()`.
- **The 1997 look**: material options `vertexSnap` and `affine`, `useFog` (by distance, and by height with `height: { top, bottom }` for pits and valleys), `usePostProcess` with `dither`, `posterize`, `paletteMatch`, `lutGrade`, `crt` (with `POST.CRT_PRESETS`) and `POST.COLOR_LEVELS`.
- **Screen effects** (each spread into `usePostProcess`, tuned by writing into `effect.uniforms`): `colorAdjust`, `mosaic`, `wave`, `shockwave`, `distort`, `rgbSplit`, `glitch`, `grain`, `oldFilm`, `halftone`, `ascii`, `blur`, `zoomBlur`, `motionBlur`, `tiltShift`, `bloom`, `godrays`, `phosphor`, `ntsc`, `lcd`. A hand-written effect can read `sampleTextureSmooth`, `sampleInput` and `sampleHistory`, and take `passes` for more than one read of the frame. In `project.json`'s `post` chain a built-in is `{ builtin: 'ascii', uniforms: { size: 12 }, options: { glyphs: ' ░▒▓█' } }`: `uniforms` for its knobs, `options` for what is written into it when made (only `ascii`'s `glyphs` today). A built-in's key is the name of its call (`paletteMatch`, `lutGrade`, `colorAdjust`; the old `palette`, `lut` and `adjust` are still read). `POST_BUILTINS[i].fields` and `MATERIAL_LOOKS[i].fields` (both from `nacatamalon/authoring`) list what each takes, with ranges. Knobs keep one name per idea: `amount` how much shows (0 untouched to 1), `intensity` a brightness that may pass 1, `size` a cell in game pixels, `scale` a multiplier, `radius` a reach in game pixels, `center` from `[0, 0]` (top left) to `[1, 1]`. Some effects already hold another's work, so stacking them does it twice: `crt` has a glow (`halation`), noise, vignette, flicker and a colour split (`convergence`); `oldFilm` grain, vignette and flicker; `glitch` a colour split; `paletteMatch` its own `dither`; `lcd` (`ghosting`) and `phosphor` both leave trails; `posterize` is `dither` with `amount: 0`. Effects laid on a grid of game pixels (mosaic, halftone, ascii, dither, grain, lcd, mangaDots) look cleanest with sizes that are multiples of one another. Order: grade first, then the world (distortions, blurs, bloom), then the palette and dither, then the screen (phosphor, ntsc, lcd, crt).
- **Pixels** (pictures painted in code): `createPixels`, `setPixel`, `getPixel`, `fillRect`, `drawLine`, `fillCircle`, `drawCircle`, `fillEllipse`, `drawEllipse`, `fillPolygon`, `drawText`, `fillGradient`, `fillNoise`, `fillChecker`, `blitPixels`, `mapPixels`, `clonePixels`, `swapColors`, `createPixelTexture`, `updatePixelTexture`, `useLoadPixels`.
- **Photos**: `useCapture` (`TPhoto`, `TPhotoOptions`, `TPhotoBox`).
- **Audio**: `useSound` (one file: effects, an ambience, a single recording; `{ src }` loads it, `{ sfx: { preset } }` makes an effect, `{ samples, sampleRate }` plays a sound worked out in code instead of Web Audio; `pan` from -1, left, to 1, right, moved with `setPan` or a tween on the handle's `pan`), `useMusic` (one piece recorded in one file or several, its layers faded in and out with `setLayer`; given its `bpm` and `firstBeat` it has `onBeat` and `beat`, and like a song `position` and `positionAt`), `useSong` (a tune written as notes, `useSong(useLoadSong({ src: '/music/x.song' }))`, made into sound by the engine's 8-bit synth; a song's `instruments` shape each note as it sounds, the way an 8-bit tracker does: `volume`, `duty`, `arpeggio` and `pitch` as lists of numbers read one a frame, a `|` where a list starts again, plus `vibrato` and `slide`; a voice starts with its `instrument`, and `@name` in its notes changes it, `@-` to none; the engine has instruments ready, `BUILTIN.MUSIC.INSTRUMENTS`: `@lead`, `@soft`, `@pluck`, `@bell`, `@major`, `@minor`, `@power`, `@stab` on the squares, `@bass` on the triangle, `@kick`, `@snare`, `@hat`, `@open-hat`, `@crash` on the noise; after a note, in brackets, what only it does: `[slide]`, `[vib]`, `[arp:0,4,7]`, `[vol:8]`; a fifth voice, `dpcm`, plays samples at the console's grain, with an instrument's `sample`: the engine's (`@drum-kick`, `@drum-snare`, `@drum-clap`, `@drum-tom`, `@orch-hit`, `@zap`) or a sound file of the game, `{ sample: '/samples/hit.wav' }`; a text export of FamiTracker or FamiStudio becomes a `.song` with `importTrackerText` from `nacatamalon/authoring`, which the editor does when one is dropped on it, or a game loads it as it is with `useLoadTrackerSong({ src: '/music/theme.txt' })`, the song `useLoadSong` gives; a song's `chip` is `'nes'` (the default), `'snes'` (voices `s1`-`s8`, each a sample: `@piano`, `@strings`, `@flute`, `@choir`…, with `adsr` and an `echo`) or `'genesis'` (FM voices `fm1`-`fm6`, each an `fm` of four operators: `@epiano`, `@slap-bass`, `@fm-brass`…, plus `psg1`-`psg3` and `psgNoise`); each voice has a `pan`, and a song's handle has `pan.<voice>` a tween can move; `song.position` is the seconds into it being heard now, `song.beat` the same in beats from the start (not `onBeat`'s beat of the bar) (by the audio clock, the speaker's delay taken off) and `song.latency` that delay, for a rhythm game; `onBeat` comes on the beat heard; `useAudio().setOffset(s)` adds the player's own delay (headphones), measured and kept by the game, and all of it counts it; the engine has thirty-nine public domain songs, `BUILTIN.MUSIC.SONGS`, by key: `useSong(useLoadSong({ src: 'nacatamalon:ode-to-joy' }))`; the whole of it, for people, is `guides/music.md` in this package; a voice that sings over a song, below), `useLoadAudio`, `useAudio` (volumes per channel), `useAudioListener`. A sound laid out in a scene document: `soundOf(box, name)` gives its controls.
- **State**: `useData`, `useWatch`, `createGameStore`, `useStore`, `createGameSignal`, `useSignal`.
- **Maths and random**: `useRandom`, `clamp`, `lerp`, `vec2Add`, `vec3Add` and the other `vec2*`/`vec3*`.
- **Whole pixels**: `createGame({ pixelSnap })`, on by default unless `smooth`: things are drawn on whole game pixels (where they are keeps its fractions).
- **Platformer camera and layers**: `useCameraFollow(hero, { deadzone: { width, height }, bounds: map, lead, smooth })` (moves in late update, whole pixels; `.shake(px, s)`, `.snap()`; `rooms: [rect, …]` or `{ width, height }` keeps it in the target's room and scrolls to the next over `scroll` s, with `onRoom` and `.scrolling`); `createBackdrop({ key, parallax: { x, y }, y })` for endless far layers; `parallax` on sprites, texts, panels and map layers (never on what is pinned to the screen), `useParallax` on objects; `repeat: true` on a sprite tiles its picture instead of stretching.
- **Platformer character with no physics**: `useTileBody2d({ width, height })`, walking on the scene's maps; same fields as `useCharacterBody2d` (`TCharacterBody2d`), which is the one that also pushes crates in a 2D world.
- **2D physics**: `installPhysics2d` and `useCharacterBody2d` from `nacatamalon/physics2d`; `usePhysicsWorld2d` and `usePhysicsBody2d` from `nacatamalon`. A scene's maps are in its world (walls, ledges, slopes). `useCharacterBody2d({ width, height })` is a platformer's character: write `velocity` (px/s) every frame; read `onGround`, `onWall`, `onCeiling`, `onOneWay` (`dropThrough()`), `onLadder` (set `climbing`), `ground`, `damage`.
- **Joints (2D)**: `useJoint2d(a, b, { type: 'hinge', at: { x, y } })` from `nacatamalon/physics2d`; types `hinge`, `rope`, `spring` (`frequency`, `damping`), `slider` (`axis`), `weld`; `b = null` pins to the world; points are world points.
- **Soft bodies (2D)**: `useSoftBody2d({ shape: 'disk', radius, polygon })` from `nacatamalon/physics2d` (also `'polygon'` with `points`, `'rope'` with `to`, `pinned`); `softness` (Hz, 5), `keepShape` (default true; false slumps like goo); keeps its object at its middle, `outline` relative to it, `push(x, y)` per frame, `kick(x, y)`. Draw it with `createPolygon({ points, texture })` from `nacatamalon`: a shape whose `points` you move every frame, picture stretched with them.
- **3D physics**: `installPhysics3d` and `useCharacterBody` from `nacatamalon/physics3d`; `usePhysicsWorld3d` and `usePhysicsBody3d` from `nacatamalon`.
- **A voice that speaks and sings** (made, not recorded), from `nacatamalon/speech`: `useSound(renderSpeech({ text: '¡Hola!' }))` (or `phonemes: 'HH AH0 L OW1 .'`; `throat` `1` a man, `1.15` a woman, `1.3` a child; `pitch`, `speed`, `melody`), `useSound(renderSinging({ notes: [{ pitch: 'C4', beats: 1, lyric: 'la' }], tempo }))`. A song's voice is a `.vocal` file apart from its `.song` (`format`, `start` the beat its first line begins, `singers` by name, `lines` of `notes` with a `lyric` each, `'can-'` a word that goes on, `who` sings a line): `useSong(accompany(useLoadVocal({ src: '/music/x.vocal' }), useLoadSong({ src: '/music/x.song' })))` sings it over the song as it plays, at its tempo and in its key, in a voice of its own, `vocal`; `lyricsAt(vocal, song.beat)?.words` is the words sung so far. Lyrics are read by rules in Spanish (`'es'`); other languages as `phonemes`. All of it is `guides/music.md`, section 10.
- **Saved scenes**: `sceneFromDoc`, `parseSceneDoc`; a box made again while the game runs: `useSpawn(boxFromDoc)(doc, place)` from a document, `useSpawn(copyBox)(box, place)` from a box a scene built.

- **React**: `Game`, `useGame`, `useGameStore`, `useSignal` from `nacatamalon/react`.

- **Checking a game from a test** (Node or Bun, no browser): `createHeadlessGame({ width, height, scenes: { Level } })` from `nacatamalon/headless`; `await game.loaded()`, then `press(key)`, `run(frames)`, `release(key)`, `tap(key)`, and look with `find(name)` (an object and its drawables), `drawn()` (each sprite, text and panel on screen: `text`, `left`, `top`, `width`, `height`, `seen`) and `scenes`. A step per frame (60 a second), `seed: 1`: the same run every time. Files come from `public/` (`assets`); PNG only for pictures; physics runs once installed as the game does (`installPhysics2d()`), and `loaded()` waits for its world; silent sound; no pointer, pad or pixels. Run frames to check what the code does rather than guessing; a scene that throws throws from `run`.

`nacatamalon/authoring` and `nacatamalon/extend` are for tools and engine extensions; a game never needs them.

## Getting help and sharing

When the person you are helping asks where to get help, hits what looks like a bug in the engine
itself, or finishes a game, these are the places:

- A bug in the engine or a feature request: https://github.com/nacatamalcore/nacatamalon/issues
- Questions and help: the Discord, https://discord.gg/jtyY3RkYTc
- Sharing a finished game: the showcase forum on that Discord. Games made with the engine:
  https://nacatamalon.com/showcase
- News: https://x.com/nacatamalcore
